definition: Humans and their extinct relatives after the split from the chimpanzee line, such as Australopithecus and Homo erectus.
Shaping stone, such as flint, by striking it so that sharp flakes break off.
A smooth, shell-shaped break typical of glassy stones like flint and obsidian; it gives very sharp edges.
The cone-shaped crack that spreads into a brittle material from the point where it is struck.
Having the same properties in every direction, with no grain or cleavage planes.
The oldest well-known stone-tool tradition (from about 2.6 million years ago): simple flakes and choppers.
A stone-tool tradition (from about 1.76 million years ago) known for symmetrical, two-sided handaxes.
A stone-tool method in which a core is carefully prepared so that one final blow removes a flake of planned shape.
How large an animal's brain is compared with the size expected for an animal of its body mass.
The energy the body uses at complete rest just to stay alive.
The swelling and breakdown of starch grains in hot water, which makes them easy to digest.
The period of African prehistory from roughly 300,000 to 40,000 years ago, when Homo sapiens appeared.
Natural earth rich in iron oxide, ground into red or yellow pigment.
The geological epoch from about 2.6 million to 11,700 years ago, the era of the ice ages.
Dating once-living material by how much radioactive carbon-14 is left in it; works back to about 50,000 years.
The time it takes for half of the atoms of a radioactive substance to decay.
Dating buried sediment or burnt stone by measuring the light released from energy stored in its crystals since it was last heated or exposed to sunlight.
Dating volcanic rock from the ratio of argon isotopes produced by the decay of potassium-40.
A numbered warm or cold phase of past climate, identified from oxygen isotopes in sea-floor sediments.
The study of what happens to remains after death: decay, burial and disturbance.
The time from one new Moon to the next: about 29.5 days.
The sequence of steps a maker follows, from raw material to finished tool.
Mesopotamian writing made by pressing a wedge-shaped reed into clay.
Counting in base 60, as the Babylonians did; we still use it for minutes, seconds and degrees.
A way of writing numbers in which a digit's value depends on its position, as in 205 versus 250.
Counting in base 20, as the Maya did.
The first morning a star becomes visible again just before sunrise, after weeks hidden in the Sun's glare.
Extra days added outside the regular months to make a 365-day year.
The 1,460-year period over which the Egyptian 365-day calendar drifted all the way round the seasons.
The Egyptian measure of a slope: horizontal run, in palms and fingers, for each cubit of height.
Three whole numbers a, b, c with a² + b² = c², such as 3, 4, 5.
The number that multiplies with another to give 1; the reciprocal of 4 is 1/4.
The science of measurement and of standard units such as weights and lengths.
An upright stick or pillar whose shadow is used to tell the time or the season.
A water clock: time is measured by water flowing into or out of a vessel.
Inserting an extra day or month into a calendar to keep it in step with the seasons.
The 19-year period after which the Moon's phases fall on almost the same dates of the solar year (19 years ≈ 235 lunar months).
An eclipse cycle of about 18 years 11 days, after which similar eclipses repeat.
A flowing, handwritten form of Egyptian hieroglyphs used on papyrus.
A stepped temple tower of ancient Mesopotamia.
The 52-year cycle formed when the Maya 260-day and 365-day calendars come back into step.
The Mesoamerican calendar that counts days from a fixed starting date far in the past.
An event believed to foretell the future, such as an eclipse read as a sign from the gods.
For early Greek thinkers, the basic stuff or first principle from which everything comes.
Anaximander's "boundless": an endless, undefined source from which all things arise.
For Heraclitus, the rational order or law behind constant change.
The idea that matter is made of tiny, indivisible particles moving in empty space.
Completely empty space.
Space completely filled with matter, leaving no empty space.
A classical Indian school of philosophy known for its theory of atoms and categories of reality.
In Indian philosophy, the ultimate indivisible particle of matter.
A classical Indian school of logic and theory of knowledge.
In Indian philosophy, a valid means of gaining knowledge, such as perception or inference.
The invariable connection between a sign and what it indicates, as between smoke and fire.
A form of argument in which a conclusion follows from two premises.
A dark room or box with a small hole; light through the hole forms an upside-down image on the opposite wall.
The Chinese "Five Phases" — wood, fire, earth, metal and water — understood as stages of continual change.
In Aristotle's cosmos, the changeable region below the Moon, made of earth, water, air and fire.
In Aristotle's cosmos, the unchanging heavens above the Moon.
In ancient cosmology, the fifth element that made up the heavens.
Explaining things by their purpose or goal: "the eye exists in order to see".
Aristotle's four kinds of explanation: what a thing is made of, its form, what produced it, and its purpose.
The working rule of science: explain natural events only by natural causes.
An ancient Greek unit of length, roughly 160–185 metres; its exact value varied.
The upward push of a fluid on an object in it, equal to the weight of fluid the object displaces.
The idea that nothing happens without a reason why it is so and not otherwise.
Proving something by showing that its opposite leads to a contradiction.
A starting statement accepted without proof, from which other results are deduced.
A basic assumption accepted without proof, especially in geometry.
A statement that has been proved from axioms or earlier results.
Two lengths are incommensurable when no common unit measures both exactly, like the side and diagonal of a square.
A number that cannot be written as a fraction of whole numbers, such as √2 or π.
A whole number greater than 1 that can be divided exactly only by 1 and itself.
A Greek technique for finding areas and volumes by squeezing them between ever-closer inner and outer shapes.
A curve made by slicing a cone with a plane: circle, ellipse, parabola or hyperbola.
A closed oval curve; planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
The U-shaped curve followed by a thrown object, ignoring air resistance.
An open curve with two branches, made by slicing a double cone steeply.
In a right triangle, the ratio of the side opposite an angle to the longest side; first tabulated as half-chords in India.
Sanskrit for "empty": the Indian name for zero.
A step-by-step procedure for solving a problem.
The branch of mathematics that uses symbols for unknown quantities and the rules for working with them.
An equation for which only whole-number solutions are wanted.
An equation of the form Nx² + 1 = y², to be solved in whole numbers.
The cyclic method of Indian mathematicians for solving Pell's equation.
A proof that a statement holds for 1, and that if it holds for one number it holds for the next — so it holds for all.
Every whole number above 1 can be written as a product of primes in only one way.
A sum with infinitely many terms that can still add up to a finite value, such as 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ….
The mathematics of continuous change: rates of change (derivatives) and accumulated totals (integrals).
An imagined quantity smaller than any positive number yet not zero; used informally in early calculus.
The instantaneous rate of change of a quantity; the slope of a curve at a point.
The total accumulated by a varying quantity; the area under a curve.
The precise definition of a limit: for any tolerance ε you can find a closeness δ that guarantees it.
A function whose graph has no breaks or jumps.
All numbers on the number line, rational and irrational, with no gaps.
A way of defining a real number as a split of the fractions into a lower and an upper set.
A consistent geometry in which Euclid's parallel postulate is false.
A non-Euclidean geometry in which many parallels pass through a point and triangle angles add to less than 180°.
Euclid's fifth postulate: through a point there is exactly one line parallel to a given line.
A space that looks flat close up but may be curved overall, like the surface of the Earth.
The mathematical rule that gives distances in a curved space.
The branch of mathematics that studies collections of objects (sets), now the usual foundation of mathematics.
The size of a set; two sets have the same cardinality if their members can be paired off exactly.
A perfect one-to-one pairing between the members of two sets.
A set is countable if its members can be listed 1, 2, 3, … (even if the list never ends).
Too large to be listed even in an endless list; the real numbers are uncountable.
The size of the set of counting numbers, the smallest infinity.
Cantor's proof that any list of real numbers misses some, by building a number that differs from each entry.
The set of all subsets of a set.
Cantor's conjecture that no infinity lies between the counting numbers and the real numbers; it can be neither proved nor disproved from the usual axioms.
The contradiction arising from "the set of all sets that do not contain themselves".
The programme of deriving all of mathematics from pure logic.
The view of mathematics as the manipulation of symbols by fixed rules.
The view that mathematical objects exist only if they can be constructed; it rejects some classical proofs.
Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice: the standard foundation of modern mathematics.
Gödel's result that any consistent system able to do arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove.
A system is consistent if it never proves both a statement and its opposite.
Whether there is a mechanical procedure that always gives a yes-or-no answer to a question.
German for "decision problem": is there an algorithm that decides whether any logical statement is valid?
An imaginary device that reads and writes symbols on a tape by fixed rules: the theoretical model of every computer.
The question of whether a program will ever stop; Turing proved no program can answer it for every case.
The large-scale translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic in Abbasid Baghdad (8th–10th centuries).
The ancient idea that the eye sees by sending out rays to objects.
The idea that we see because light or images travel from objects into the eye.
A hand-held instrument for measuring the height of stars and the Sun and solving astronomical problems.
The small angle by which the visible horizon lies below the true horizontal when seen from a height.
A hospital in the medieval Islamic world.
The part of a clock that releases its driving power in small, regular steps.
A model of the heavens made of rings for the main circles of the sky.
The angle between the direction a compass points and true north.
The three language arts of the medieval curriculum: grammar, rhetoric and logic.
The four mathematical arts of the medieval curriculum: arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy.
A formal medieval debate in which a question was argued for and against before a master resolved it.
A body accelerating evenly from rest covers the same distance as one moving all the time at its average speed.
In old astronomy, a small circle whose centre moves round a larger circle (the deferent), used to model planetary motion.
In old astronomy, the large circle that carries a planet's epicycle.
In Ptolemy's astronomy, an off-centre point about which a planet moves at a steady angular rate.
Two circles, one rolling inside another twice its size, that turn circular motion into straight-line motion.
A line of Indian astronomer-mathematicians (14th–16th centuries) who found infinite series for π and trigonometric functions.
With the Sun at the centre.
With the Earth at the centre.
The apparent backward loop of a planet across the stars, caused by the Earth overtaking it.
The apparent shift of an object against its background when seen from two different places.
The explosion of a star, which can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.
Tycho Brahe's model: the Sun and Moon circle the Earth, while the other planets circle the Sun.
The tendency of a body to keep doing what it is doing — stay at rest or keep moving in a straight line.
The 17th-century view of nature as matter in motion, like a machine.
A "crucial experiment" that decides between rival theories.
How strongly a ray of light is bent (refracted) when it passes into another material.
The bending of light as it passes from one material into another.
Newton's name for the rate of change of a flowing quantity — what we call a derivative.
Newton's law that every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to their masses and inversely to the square of their distance.
Properties thought to belong to objects themselves, such as size, shape and motion.
Properties that exist in our perception, such as colour, taste and warmth.
The pre-modern art of transforming matter, including attempts to turn base metals into gold.
The change of one substance — or, in biology, one species — into another.
A still-head used in distillation to collect and cool vapour.
Separating liquids by boiling them and condensing the vapour.
The powdery residue left after heating a metal in air — what we now call a metal oxide.
An imagined substance once thought to be released when things burn.
Paracelsus's three principles of matter: sulfur, mercury and salt.
Medicine based on chemistry, as promoted by Paracelsus.
The 18th-century study of gases.
The old name for carbon dioxide.
Priestley's name for oxygen.
In a chemical reaction, the total mass of what you start with equals the total mass of what you end with.
A substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means.
When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in small whole-number ratios.
The mass of an atom of an element compared with a standard, such as hydrogen = 1.
The mass of a substance that combines with a fixed mass of a standard, such as 8 grams of oxygen.
Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
Two or more atoms bonded together; the smallest unit of a compound.
Made of two atoms, as in the oxygen molecule O₂.
Breaking down a compound by passing an electric current through it.
Berzelius's theory that compounds are made of a positively and a negatively charged part.
The properties of the elements repeat regularly when they are arranged in order — now known to be by atomic number.
The number of protons in an atom's nucleus, which fixes its place in the periodic table.
The idea that complex things can be fully explained by their simpler parts.
Properties of a whole that its parts do not have on their own, such as the wetness of water.
The old idea that all things form a fixed ladder from minerals up through plants and animals to humans, angels and God.
Finding evidence for God's design in the natural world.
Naming each species with two Latin words — genus and species — as in Homo sapiens.
The science of naming and classifying living things.
The idea that the Earth's history was shaped mainly by sudden, violent events.
The idea that the Earth was shaped by the same slow processes we see today, acting over long times.
The immense age of the Earth, measured in millions and billions of years.
Rock layers contain fossils in a reliable order, so fossils can be used to match and date layers.
A fossil typical of a particular age, used to identify rock layers.
All living things are made of cells, and all cells come from other cells.
The idea that living things contain a special life force not found in non-living matter.
The process by which inherited traits that help survival and reproduction become more common over generations.
The rapid branching of one ancestral species into many, each suited to a different way of life.
The idea that all living things share ancestors, forming one branching tree of life.
The idea that characteristics acquired during life can be passed to offspring.
The old idea that offspring traits are a mixture of the parents', like mixing paints.
Darwin's mistaken theory that particles from every part of the body gather in the reproductive cells.
The old idea that living things can arise directly from non-living matter.
The theory that many diseases are caused by microorganisms.
Four criteria for showing that a particular microbe causes a particular disease.
A unit of heredity: a stretch of DNA that carries information for a trait.
One of the different versions of a gene.
An allele whose effect shows even when only one copy is present.
An allele whose effect shows only when two copies are present.
The particular set of alleles an organism carries.
The observable characteristics of an organism.
Mendel's rule that the two copies of a gene separate when reproductive cells form.
Mendel's rule that different genes are inherited independently of one another (when on different chromosomes).
A thread-like structure in the cell nucleus made of DNA and protein, carrying many genes.
Cell division that produces two identical cells.
Cell division that halves the number of chromosomes, producing eggs or sperm.
The tendency of genes close together on a chromosome to be inherited together.
The exchange of segments between paired chromosomes during meiosis.
A virus that infects bacteria.
Working out a structure from the pattern X-rays make when they scatter off it.
The matching of DNA bases across the double helix: A with T, and G with C.
DNA copying in which each new double helix keeps one old strand and gains one new one.
A group of three DNA or RNA bases that codes for one amino acid or a stop signal.
Crick's rule that genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein, not back from protein.
An enzyme that copies RNA into DNA, used by retroviruses such as HIV.
Using the roughly steady build-up of mutations to estimate when species diverged.
Apparent purpose in living things that results from natural selection rather than conscious design.
Reproduction of seeds without fertilisation, giving offspring identical to the parent.
The origin of life from non-living matter.
An imagined weightless fluid once thought to be heat itself.
Weightless substances once used to explain heat, light, electricity and magnetism.
The science of heat, work, energy and their transformations.
An ideal heat-engine cycle with the highest possible efficiency between two temperatures.
An idealised, infinitely slow process that could be run backwards without any loss.
Taking place at constant temperature.
Taking place with no heat flowing in or out.
The fraction of heat put into an engine that comes out as useful work.
The amount of work that produces a given amount of heat; about 4.18 joules per calorie.
Energy can change form but is never created or destroyed: the First Law of Thermodynamics.
A measure of disorder — of how many microscopic arrangements match what we see — which tends to increase.
In an isolated system, entropy never decreases; heat flows from hot to cold by itself.
Temperature measured from absolute zero (−273.15 °C), in kelvins.
An early device for storing electric charge: a glass jar coated with metal inside and out.
The first battery: a stack of metal discs separated by brine-soaked card.
A liquid or paste that conducts electricity by the movement of ions.
The interconnected phenomena of electricity and magnetism.
A coil of wire that acts like a bar magnet when current flows through it.
Producing an electric current by changing the magnetic field through a circuit.
An induced current always flows so as to oppose the change that produced it.
A machine that turns motion into electric current.
A physical quantity spread through space, such as the electric or magnetic field.
Faraday's picture of a field as lines showing the direction of the force at each point.
Maxwell's term for the effect of a changing electric field, which produces a magnetic field just as a current does.
An imagined invisible medium once thought to fill space and carry light waves.
A wave of electric and magnetic fields travelling at the speed of light; light and radio are examples.
The four equations that describe all of classical electricity, magnetism and light.
Explaining heat and the behaviour of matter from the statistics of huge numbers of molecules.
One exact arrangement of all the molecules in a system.
The theory that gases are made of moving molecules whose collisions produce pressure and temperature.
An ideal object that absorbs all light falling on it; it glows with a spectrum that depends only on its temperature.
The absurd classical prediction that a hot object should radiate infinite energy at short wavelengths.
The classical rule that energy is shared equally among all the ways a system can move.
The smallest possible packet of something, such as energy in light.
The fundamental constant h that links the energy of a light quantum to its frequency: E = hν.
A particle, or quantum, of light.
The release of electrons from a metal when light shines on it.
The minimum energy needed to pull an electron out of a metal.
Einstein's 1905 theory: the laws of physics and the speed of light are the same for all steadily moving observers.
A viewpoint that is not accelerating, in which objects with no force on them move in straight lines.
The slowing of moving clocks, as seen by an observer they are moving past.
The shortening of moving objects along their direction of motion.
The quantity γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²) that sets how much time slows and lengths shrink.
Space and time combined into one four-dimensional whole.
Einstein's E = mc²: mass is a form of energy.
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom.
A helium nucleus — two protons and two neutrons — given off by some radioactive atoms.
A sharp, bright or dark line in a spectrum at a wavelength characteristic of an element.
The constant in the formula for the wavelengths of hydrogen's spectral lines.
An electron's sudden change from one energy level to another, emitting or absorbing a photon.
The fact that light and matter behave both as waves and as particles.
The wavelength of a moving particle: Planck's constant divided by its momentum.
The mathematical description of a quantum system; its square gives the probability of each outcome.
The rule that the square of the wavefunction gives the probability of finding a particle at a place.
Heisenberg's principle that position and momentum cannot both be known exactly at once.
The effects of gravity cannot be told apart from the effects of acceleration.
Einstein's 1915 theory of gravity as the curvature of spacetime.
Bohr and Heisenberg's view that a quantum system has no definite properties until it is measured.
A quantum state that is a combination of several possible states at once.
A link between quantum particles so that measuring one instantly fixes what will be found for the other.
Proposed extra quantities that would fix the results of quantum measurements in advance.
Bell's proof that no theory of local hidden variables can reproduce all predictions of quantum mechanics.
The loss of quantum behaviour when a system interacts with its surroundings.
An instrument that splits light into two beams and recombines them, so tiny differences in path show up as interference fringes.
The branch of philosophy that studies knowledge: what it is and how we get it.
The branch of philosophy that studies what exists.
The view that knowledge comes mainly from experience and observation.
Reasoning from particular observations to a general rule.
Reasoning in which the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises.
Hume's puzzle: past experience cannot logically guarantee that the future will be like the past.
The 1920s–30s movement holding that only logically or empirically checkable statements are meaningful.
The positivist rule that a statement is meaningful only if it can be checked by logic or experience.
Popper's test of a scientific theory: it must say what observations could prove it wrong.
The question of how to tell science from non-science.
The valid argument: if H, then E; not E; therefore not H.
In Kuhn's sense, the shared theories, methods and examples that guide a scientific community.
Kuhn's term for everyday research that solves puzzles within an accepted paradigm.
An observation that does not fit the accepted theory.
A scientific revolution in which one paradigm replaces another.
Lakatos's term for a series of developing theories sharing a common core.
In Lakatos's account, the central assumptions of a research programme that scientists protect.
In Lakatos's account, the adjustable auxiliary assumptions around a programme's hard core.
An extra assumption needed to connect a theory to an observation.
Feyerabend's view that no single fixed method governs scientific progress.
A hypothesis is never tested alone but together with many background assumptions, so a failed test does not show which one is wrong.
When the available evidence is not enough to decide between rival theories.
The view that our beliefs face experience as a connected whole, not one at a time.
Treating degrees of belief as probabilities and updating them with Bayes' theorem as evidence comes in.
How likely a hypothesis seems before the new evidence is considered.
How likely a hypothesis seems after taking the new evidence into account.
The view that successful scientific theories are at least approximately true, including about unobservable things.
The view that theories are tools for prediction, not literal descriptions of reality.
The argument that the success of science would be a miracle unless its theories were roughly true.
The argument that because many successful past theories proved false, today's may too.
The view that science reliably captures the mathematical structure of the world, even if not its underlying nature.
Van Fraassen's view that science aims only at theories that are correct about what can be observed.
The discovery, in the 2010s, that many published findings could not be reproduced.
Trying many analyses until one gives a "statistically significant" result.
The tendency for positive results to be published while null results go unpublished.
The chance that a study will detect a real effect of a given size.
Publicly recording a study's hypotheses and analysis plan before collecting the data.
Kuhn's claim that rival paradigms lack a fully shared standard or vocabulary for comparing them.
A machine that moves by itself once set going, often imitating a person or animal. Plural: automata.
A machine whose behaviour is set by a changeable pattern of instructions (pins, pegs, punched holes or code), so the same machine can do different jobs.
A stiff card in which the presence or absence of holes stores instructions or data, first used to control looms and later computers.
A way of writing numbers using only the digits 0 and 1. Digital computers store everything in binary.
A way of calculating a table of values for a formula such as n × n using only addition, by building each new value from the differences between earlier ones.
George Boole's algebra of logic, in which statements are true (1) or false (0) and are combined with AND, OR and NOT.
A simple circuit that carries out one logical rule, such as AND, OR or NOT, on true/false (1/0) signals.
A machine that can carry out tasks by itself. The word comes from Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R., from the Czech robota, forced labour.
A computing system made of many simple connected units, loosely modelled on brain cells, whose connection strengths can be adjusted so that it learns.
A nerve cell that receives signals and, if they are strong enough, fires a signal of its own. In AI, a simple unit that imitates this.
Frank Rosenblatt’s 1950s learning machine: an artificial neuron (or layer of them) whose weights are adjusted after each mistake.
Alan Turing’s 1950 'imitation game': a judge holds typed conversations and tries to tell a machine from a person.
The study of feedback, communication and control in animals and machines, founded by Norbert Wiener in 1948.
A rule of thumb that usually helps find a good answer quickly, without guaranteeing the best one.
Making computers improve at a task through experience or examples, rather than by being given every rule.
Learning by trial and error, where actions that lead to rewards become more likely and those that lead to penalties less likely.
A computer design in which the instructions are kept in the machine’s memory alongside the data, so a new program can be loaded easily.
A period when disappointment after hype leads to sharp cuts in funding and interest in artificial intelligence.
A program that stores a human expert’s knowledge as many IF–THEN rules and chains them together to give advice.
People’s tendency to read real understanding and feeling into a machine that produces human-sounding words.
A small, simplified setting, such as a table of blocks, in which an AI program can be tested because everything is precisely defined.
'Exclusive or': a rule that outputs 1 when exactly one of two inputs is on. A single perceptron cannot learn it.
A layer of artificial neurons between a network’s inputs and its output, allowing it to learn patterns a single layer cannot.
The way the number of possibilities to check grows astronomically as a problem gets bigger.
The observation that skills easy for a small child, like seeing and moving, are much harder for computers than skills like chess or algebra.
The puzzle of how a reasoning program can know what stays the same when it acts, without checking every fact.
The method for training neural networks that passes the error backwards from the output, working out how to adjust every weight to reduce it.
Improving a model step by step by adjusting it slightly in whichever direction reduces its error most, like walking downhill in fog.
How big a step a learning method takes each time it adjusts its weights.
A neural network that slides small learned filters across an image, so a pattern is recognised wherever it appears.
When a model learns the quirks and noise of its training examples so closely that it does badly on new data.
Examples kept back during training and used only to measure how well a model works on data it has never seen.
A simple probabilistic classifier that adds up evidence from each feature (such as each word) as if they were independent.
A learning method that separates two classes with the boundary that leaves the widest possible gap between them.
A learning method that trains many decision trees on random samples of the data and lets them vote.
The problem that, in a deep network, the error signal shrinks as it is passed backwards, so early layers barely learn.
Machine learning with neural networks that have many layers, each learning more abstract features than the last.
Graphics processing unit: a chip with thousands of small processors working in parallel, first built for video games and now used to train neural networks.
A simple way for an artificial neuron to respond: output zero for negative inputs and pass positive inputs straight through.
A training trick that randomly switches off some neurons each time, so the network can’t rely on any one of them and overfits less.
A list of numbers representing a word as a point in space, learned from text so that words with similar meanings lie close together.
In neural networks, a mechanism that lets the model weigh which parts of its input matter most for the output it is producing right now.
A pair of networks trained against each other: a generator that makes fakes and a discriminator that tries to spot them.
An input changed in tiny, carefully chosen ways that makes a neural network confidently give a wrong answer.
Training a game-playing program by having it play against copies of itself and learn from the results.
The way a chain of amino acids folds into a precise 3-D shape, which determines what the protein does.
A neural-network design, introduced in 2017, that processes all the words of a text at once using self-attention. The basis of modern language models.
The mechanism in a transformer by which each word weighs how relevant every other word in the passage is to its meaning.
A model trained to predict the next piece of text given what came before. Large language models (LLMs) do this with billions of parameters.
The first, large-scale stage of training a model on huge amounts of unlabelled data, before it is adapted to particular tasks.
Further training of a pre-trained model on a smaller, specific dataset to adapt it to a particular job or style.
Regular relationships showing how a model’s error falls as its size, training data and computing power increase.
A language model’s ability to pick up a new task from instructions or examples given in its prompt, without retraining.
Prompting or training a model to write out intermediate reasoning steps before giving its answer.
An image generator that learns to remove noise step by step, so it can turn random noise into a picture guided by a description.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a model to give answers that a reward model, learned from people’s rankings, scores highly.
A model trained to predict which of several answers people would prefer, used to guide another model’s training.
When an AI model confidently states something false or made up, such as an invented fact or reference.
Able to take in or produce more than one kind of data, such as text, images, audio and video.
An AI model whose trained weights are published so anyone can download, run and modify it.
A language model trained to work through a problem in a long chain of reasoning before giving its answer.
Improving an AI’s answer by making several independent attempts and taking the most common result.
An AI system that carries out multi-step tasks by planning, using tools, checking results and deciding what to do next.
An attack in which hidden instructions placed in text an AI reads (such as a web page or email) trick it into doing something unintended.
METR’s measure of AI progress: the length of task, in skilled-human time, that an AI agent can complete with a given success rate.
A realistic fake image, video or voice recording of a real person, made with AI.
An AI model’s tendency to tell people what they want to hear rather than what is accurate.
Artificial general intelligence: AI that could do most intellectual tasks as well as a capable human, across many fields. There is no agreed definition.
The challenge of making sure AI systems reliably do what their designers and users actually intend, and act in line with human values.
When an AI system meets the literal goal it was given in a way its designers did not intend, exploiting a loophole in the reward.
Research into how AI models work internally, to understand what they are doing and why.
Deliberately trying to make an AI system misbehave or reveal dangerous abilities, to find weaknesses before others do.
An experiment comparing people with and without AI help, to measure how much AI actually increases their ability to do something.
The European Union’s law regulating artificial intelligence by level of risk, in force since August 2024.
The way the existence of convincing fakes lets people dismiss genuine evidence as fake.
The distance all the way round a circle or sphere.
One sixtieth of a degree of angle. A full circle has 360 degrees, or 21,600 arcminutes.
Surveying by measuring one baseline accurately and finding all other distances from angles in a chain of triangles.
In surveying, a line whose length is measured directly and accurately, from which other distances are calculated.
The small angle by which the horizon appears below the true level when seen from a height, because the Earth curves away.
The moment when the Sun is highest in the sky at a given place; usually not exactly 12:00 by the clock.
How much a planet is squashed at the poles: the difference between its equatorial and polar radii divided by the equatorial radius. For Earth, about 1 part in 298.
Squashed at the poles and bulging at the equator, like the Earth.
The north–south distance over which the height of the Pole Star changes by one degree; about 111 km, slightly longer near the poles.
An imaginary line on the Earth’s surface running due north–south from pole to pole.
A surveying instrument with a telescope for measuring horizontal and vertical angles precisely.
The true shape of the Earth as defined by mean sea level extended under the continents; lumpy because of uneven mass inside the Earth.
When the Moon passes through the Earth’s shadow, so the full Moon darkens and often turns a coppery red.
A reflector, often made of corner-cube prisms, that sends light straight back towards its source whatever angle it arrives at.
The point in the Moon’s (or a satellite’s) orbit where it is closest to the Earth.
The point in the Moon’s (or a satellite’s) orbit where it is furthest from the Earth.
A place in the DNA where a short sequence, usually four letters, is repeated a number of times that varies between people; the main markers used in DNA profiling.
A specific location in the DNA, such as an STR marker. Plural: loci.
PCR: a laboratory method that copies a chosen piece of DNA millions of times by repeatedly heating and cooling it with enzymes.
Separating DNA pieces by length by pulling them with an electric field through a thin gel-filled tube; shorter pieces move faster.
The graph of peaks produced by capillary electrophoresis; each peak is a DNA piece of a particular length.
The allele a child must have inherited from the biological father, because the mother does not carry it.
For one DNA marker, how many times more likely the results are if the tested man is the father than if a random unrelated man is.
The documented record of who collected, handled and stored a sample, needed for it to be accepted as legal evidence.
The ability of light waves to keep a steady phase relationship, so that they can interfere and form fringes.
The largest path difference over which two parts of a light beam can still interfere; roughly the wavelength squared divided by the spectral width.
The adding together of two or more waves, giving bright bands where crests meet crests and dark bands where crests meet troughs.
A random pattern of bright and dark grains formed when coherent light is scattered by a rough surface or a random medium.
The spread of brightness in a speckle pattern divided by its average; 1 for fully developed speckle.
Two parallel, partly reflecting surfaces that make light interfere with itself; also an accidental one formed by any window or plate.
A measure of the range of angles a lens or fibre accepts; larger values give finer detail and smaller speckle grains.
Thin layers on an optical surface designed so that reflected waves cancel, reducing the reflection.
A one-way valve for light, using the Faraday effect and polarisers to block light travelling backwards.
The angle of incidence at which light polarised in the plane of incidence is not reflected; about 56° for glass.
A lens and a small pinhole used to remove unwanted scattered light from a laser beam, leaving a smooth beam.
A light-absorbing trap used to safely catch unwanted laser beams and reflections.
Fluctuations caused by speckle inside a multimode optical fibre when the fibre moves or changes temperature.
An optical fibre with a core wide enough to carry light along many different paths, or modes.
An optical fibre with built-in stress that preserves one direction of polarisation.
Measuring only the part of a signal that rises and falls at the frequency at which the light source is switched, rejecting other light and noise.
The average distance between the Earth and the Sun, now defined as exactly 149,597,870,700 metres. Symbol: AU.
The angle the Earth’s radius makes as seen from the Sun, about 8.79 seconds of arc; historically the way the Sun’s distance was expressed.
A rare event when Venus passes directly between the Earth and the Sun and is seen as a black dot crossing the Sun.
A dark band that seems to join Venus to the Sun’s edge during a transit, caused mainly by optical blurring and limb darkening; it made contact times uncertain.
The square of a planet’s orbital period is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the Sun.
One sixtieth of a minute of arc, or 1/3600 of a degree: the width of a coin seen from about 5 km.
The time when a planet is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, and usually at its closest and brightest.
The speed at which light travels in a vacuum: exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, by the definition of the metre. Symbol: c.
A small shift in the apparent direction of stars caused by the Earth’s motion through their light, like tilting an umbrella when walking through rain.
A wave pattern that stays in place, with fixed points of strong and weak vibration, formed when waves bounce back and forth.
A closed metal box in which microwaves bounce back and forth and build up only at particular frequencies set by its size.
The number G in Newton’s law of gravity, setting how strongly two masses attract: about 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻².
The rate at which falling objects speed up near a body’s surface; about 9.8 m/s² on Earth. Symbol: g.
A rod hung from a thin wire or fibre, which twists slightly when tiny forces act on the rod; used to measure very small forces.
A weight hung on a string, which hangs along the local direction of gravity: the vertical.
A line on a map joining points of equal height above sea level.
The way the Earth’s crust floats on the denser rock beneath, so that mountains have deep roots of lighter rock, like icebergs in water.
Mass divided by volume; how much matter is packed into a given space. Water has a density of 1 g/cm³.
Finding the age of a rock or object by comparing the amounts of a radioactive element and the atoms it decays into.
One of the forms of a chemical element that differ in the number of neutrons in their nuclei, and so in mass, such as uranium-235 and uranium-238.
A hard, durable mineral that traps uranium but almost no lead when it forms, making it an excellent natural clock.
An instrument that separates atoms or molecules by mass using electric and magnetic fields, so they can be counted.
The carrying of heat by a moving fluid, such as hot rock slowly rising inside the Earth.
The average time a substance stays in a reservoir, such as sodium in the sea, before being removed.
The default assumption in a statistical test that there is no effect or no difference; written H0.
The hypothesis that there is a real effect or difference; written H1.
The probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of getting data at least as extreme as those observed. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
A label for results with a p-value below a chosen threshold α, often 0.05. It does not mean the effect is large or important.
The threshold α below which a p-value is called significant; also the false-alarm rate accepted when there is no effect.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis: a false alarm.
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis: missing a real effect.
A measure of how large a difference or relationship is, independent of sample size, such as Cohen’s d or Cliff’s delta.
An effect size: the probability that a value from one group is larger than a value from the other, minus the reverse. It runs from −1 to +1 and is robust to outliers.
An effect size: the difference between two means divided by the pooled standard deviation.
A range of plausible values for a quantity, calculated by a method that captures the true value in a stated share (such as 95%) of repeated experiments.
The expected proportion of false positives among all results declared significant; FDR.
The smallest false discovery rate at which a test would be declared significant; the FDR counterpart of a p-value.
A test that builds the null distribution by repeatedly shuffling group labels and recomputing the statistic.
A way of estimating uncertainty by repeatedly resampling the data with replacement.
A table counting a classifier’s correct and incorrect predictions for each class: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives in the binary case.
A positive case correctly predicted as positive.
A negative case wrongly predicted as positive: a false alarm.
A positive case wrongly predicted as negative: a miss.
Sensitivity or recall: the share of actual positives correctly identified, TP/(TP+FN).
The share of actual negatives correctly identified, TN/(TN+FP). Also called true negative rate.
Precision: the share of positive predictions that are correct, TP/(TP+FP).
The average of sensitivity and specificity (or of the recalls of all classes), which gives each class equal weight.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall, 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN). It ignores true negatives.
The correlation between predicted and actual classes, from −1 to +1, using all four cells of the confusion matrix; MCC.
A plot of true positive rate against false positive rate as the decision threshold varies; short for receiver operating characteristic.
Area under the ROC curve: the probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored higher than a randomly chosen negative.
A plot of precision against recall as the threshold varies; more informative than the ROC curve when positives are rare.
Averaging a metric over classes with equal weight per class.
Computing a metric from the pooled counts of all classes, so every prediction counts equally; micro-F1 equals accuracy in single-label problems.
The mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and actual outcomes (0 or 1); lower is better.
The average absolute difference between predictions and true values; MAE.
The square root of the average squared error; RMSE. Penalises large errors more than MAE.
R²: the share of variation in the true values explained by a model, relative to always predicting the mean.
The share of cases that are actually positive; the base rate.
ECE: the average gap between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies, measuring how well a model’s probabilities can be trusted.
Numbers and graphs that summarise a data set: its centre, spread and shape.
Whether data are nominal (unordered categories), ordinal (ordered categories), interval (equal gaps, arbitrary zero) or ratio (equal gaps, true zero).
The sum of the values divided by how many there are: the everyday average.
The middle value of sorted data; half the values lie below it. Robust to outliers.
The n-th root of the product of n values; the right average for growth rates and ratios.
The reciprocal of the mean of reciprocals; the right average for rates over equal amounts.
The mean after discarding a fixed share of the smallest and largest values.
A mean in which each value is multiplied by a weight reflecting its importance or precision.
The square root of the variance: roughly the typical distance of values from their mean.
The average squared deviation from the mean; for a sample, the sum of squared deviations divided by n − 1.
The range of the middle 50% of the data: third quartile minus first quartile (IQR).
The median of the distances of the values from their median (MAD): a robust measure of spread.
The standard deviation divided by the mean, often as a percentage.
The value below which a given percentage of the data falls.
One of the three values that split sorted data into four equal parts.
A plot of the median, quartiles and range of data, with possible outliers marked individually.
A bar chart of how many values fall into each of a series of equal intervals.
A measure of how asymmetric a distribution is; positive when there is a long tail to the right.
A measure of how heavy the tails of a distribution are, i.e. how prone it is to extreme values.
A value that lies unusually far from the rest of the data.
Dividing by n − 1 instead of n when computing a sample variance, to remove its bias.
The number of independent values that are free to vary in a calculation; for a sample variance, n − 1.
A quantity whose value depends on chance, such as the total of two dice or a noisy measurement.
A description of the possible values of a random variable and how likely each is.
The long-run average of a random variable: each possible value weighted by its probability.
Events where the outcome of one does not change the probability of the other.
The distribution of the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same probability.
The distribution of counts of rare, independent events in a fixed interval; its mean and variance are equal.
The distribution of waiting times between random events occurring at a constant rate.
The symmetric, bell-shaped distribution described by a mean and standard deviation; also called Gaussian.
A right-skewed distribution whose logarithm is normally distributed.
The number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean: z = (x − μ)/σ.
Random fluctuations in counts of discrete particles such as photons or electrons, with standard deviation equal to the square root of the mean count.
As the number of trials grows, observed frequencies and averages approach the true probabilities and means.
Sums and averages of many independent random values are approximately normally distributed, whatever the original distribution.
The standard deviation of an estimate such as a sample mean; for the mean, σ/√n.
A plot of sorted data against the quantiles expected from a reference distribution, used to check normality.
The mistaken belief that after a run of one outcome, the opposite outcome becomes more likely.
A number that quantifies doubt about a measurement result: a range in which the true value is believed to lie, at a stated confidence.
An error that shifts every reading in the same way, such as a miscalibrated instrument; averaging cannot remove it.
An error that varies unpredictably from reading to reading; it can be reduced by repeating and averaging.
How close the average of many measurements is to the true value; the absence of systematic error.
Evaluating an uncertainty component by statistics on repeated observations, for example the standard error of the mean.
Evaluating an uncertainty component from other information, such as certificates, specifications or instrument resolution.
The total standard uncertainty of a result, found by combining all components, usually in quadrature.
The combined standard uncertainty multiplied by a coverage factor k, often 2, to give an interval of about 95% confidence.
The multiplier k used to turn a combined standard uncertainty into an expanded uncertainty.
A table listing every source of uncertainty in a measurement, its size and its contribution to the total.
Working out the uncertainty of a calculated result from the uncertainties of the quantities used to calculate it.
√(χ²/(n − 1)) for a set of measurements combined by weighted mean; values much larger than 1 signal inconsistent results.
A fitted relation between an instrument’s signal and known standards, used to convert the signal of an unknown into a value.
The smallest amount that can be reliably distinguished from a blank, often 3 × the blank standard deviation divided by the calibration slope.
The smallest amount that can be measured with acceptable precision, often 10 × the blank standard deviation divided by the calibration slope.
The property of a measurement linked to the SI units through an unbroken, documented chain of calibrations.
A rule for calculating an estimate of a population parameter from sample data.
An estimator whose average over many samples equals the true value of the parameter.
The distribution of a statistic, such as the sample mean, over all possible samples of the same size.
A bell-shaped distribution with heavier tails than the normal, used for means when the standard deviation is estimated from a small sample.
A confidence interval for a proportion that keeps close to its stated coverage even for small samples.
An “exact” confidence interval for a proportion that never covers less than its stated level, at the cost of extra width.
If an event is seen in none of n trials, a 95% upper limit for its probability is about 3/n.
A comparison of two means that does not assume the groups have equal variances.
Calculating the sample size needed to detect an effect of a chosen size with a chosen power and significance level.
A range expected to contain the next single observation, wider than a confidence interval for the mean.
A range expected, with stated confidence, to contain a stated fraction of the whole population.
In Bayesian statistics, a range with a stated probability of containing the parameter, given the data and a prior.
A method for testing whether several group means differ, by comparing variation between groups with variation within them.
The rising chance of at least one false positive when many statistical tests are carried out.
The probability of at least one false positive among a family of statistical tests.
The sum of squared deviations from a mean; ANOVA splits the total sum of squares into between-group and within-group parts.
A sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom; an estimate of variance.
The ratio of the between-group to the within-group mean square in an ANOVA; near 1 when groups do not differ.
The distribution of a ratio of two independent variance estimates, used to obtain p-values in ANOVA.
The share of the total variation explained by the groups in an ANOVA: SS between ÷ SS total.
A less biased version of eta squared for estimating the effect size in an ANOVA.
The difference between an observed value and the value predicted by a model, such as its group mean.
A test of whether several groups have equal variances, using absolute deviations from each group’s centre.
A one-way ANOVA that does not assume equal variances in the groups.
A rank-based alternative to one-way ANOVA that does not assume normal data.
Tukey’s honestly significant difference: a method for comparing all pairs of group means with a joint error rate.
Testing each of m comparisons at level α/m to keep the chance of any false positive at most α.
A step-down multiple-testing correction that is always at least as powerful as Bonferroni’s.
A method for comparing several treatments with a single control group.
A 0/1 variable used to represent membership of a group in a regression model.
The framework that includes t-tests, ANOVA and linear regression as special cases.
An experiment in which every level of each factor is combined with every level of the others.
The effect of one factor averaged over the levels of the other factors.
When the effect of one factor depends on the level of another factor.
A plot of mean responses for each combination of two factors; non-parallel lines indicate an interaction.
The effect of one factor at a single level of another factor.
An effect size for one term in a multi-factor ANOVA: SS effect ÷ (SS effect + SS residual).
Grouping experimental runs into similar sets (blocks) and including the block in the analysis to remove nuisance variation.
A design in which every treatment appears once in each block, in random order within the block.
A design in which the same experimental units are measured under several conditions or at several times.
The assumption in repeated-measures ANOVA that the differences between all pairs of conditions have equal variances.
A reduction in the degrees of freedom of a repeated-measures ANOVA when sphericity is violated.
An ANOVA that also adjusts for a continuous covariate, comparing groups at the same covariate value.
A continuous variable that affects the response but is not the main interest, included in a model to adjust for it.
A factor whose levels were chosen deliberately; conclusions apply only to those levels.
A factor whose levels are a sample from a larger population, such as subjects, days or batches.
The smallest unit to which a treatment is independently applied; it determines the number of true replicates.
Treating measurements that are not independent, such as many cells from one animal, as if they were independent replicates.
The share of the total variation due to differences between groups such as tanks, animals or days.
A regression model with both fixed effects and random effects, used for grouped or repeated data.
The standard method for estimating variance components in mixed models.
A graph with one variable on each axis and one point per observation, used to see relationships.
A measure of how two variables vary together; positive when they tend to rise together. Its size depends on the units.
r: a unit-free measure of linear association between two variables, from −1 to +1.
z = ½ ln((1 + r)/(1 − r)), which makes a correlation coefficient approximately normal for confidence intervals.
Spearman’s ρ: the Pearson correlation of the ranks, measuring monotonic association.
A rank correlation based on how many pairs of observations are in the same order on both variables.
Four data sets with identical summary statistics but very different scatter plots, showing why data must be plotted.
Fitting a model by choosing parameters that minimise the sum of squared residuals.
The region around a fitted line where the true line probably lies.
The region around a fitted line where a new single observation would probably fall; wider than the confidence band.
The tendency of extreme measurements to be followed by less extreme ones when two measurements are imperfectly correlated.
Unequal scatter of the residuals, for example scatter that grows with the response.
In regression, how far a point lies from the others in x, and hence how strongly it can pull the fitted line.
A measure of how much a regression fit would change if one observation were removed.
Using a fitted calibration line backwards to estimate x from a measured y.
Regression with several predictor variables, each coefficient giving its effect with the others held fixed.
A variable related to both the presumed cause and the effect, which can create or hide an apparent relationship.
Strong correlation between predictor variables, which makes their separate effects hard to estimate.
χ² divided by the degrees of freedom of a weighted fit; close to 1 when the model and the uncertainties are right.
A model for binary outcomes in which the log-odds of the outcome is a linear function of the predictors.
The natural logarithm of the odds p/(1 − p); also called the logit.
The factor by which the odds of an outcome are multiplied, for example per unit increase in a predictor.
An association that appears in combined data but reverses or disappears within groups.
Categories with no natural order, such as species or blood group.
Categories with a natural order but no fixed spacing, such as mild, moderate and severe.
A table counting observations in each combination of two or more categorical variables.
A test comparing observed counts with expected counts using Σ(O − E)²/E.
A test of whether observed counts agree with those predicted by a theory or distribution.
The count predicted in a category or cell if the null hypothesis were true.
An exact test for a 2 × 2 table, based on the probabilities of all tables with the same row and column totals.
A correction that reduces each |O − E| by 0.5 in a 2 × 2 χ² test; it tends to be conservative.
A test for paired yes/no data, using only the pairs in which the two classifications disagree.
The ratio of the probability of an outcome in one group to that in another; also called relative risk.
The reciprocal of the difference in proportions: how many units must be treated for one extra success.
A way of combining 2 × 2 tables from several strata into one adjusted odds ratio and test.
More variation in counts than a Poisson model predicts; the variance exceeds the mean.
A regression model for counts in which the logarithm of the expected rate is a linear function of predictors.
A family of regression models, including linear, logistic and Poisson regression, linked by a common framework.
A test for a steady rise or fall in a proportion across ordered groups.
A measure of agreement between two raters corrected for the agreement expected by chance.
Splitting a continuous variable into two categories, such as high and low; it loses information and power.
